title-group.article-title: Longitudinal analysis of tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy outcomes and BCR‐ABL1 transcript decline velocity in chronic myeloid leukemia: A 16‐year real‐world study

sec.title: Background
sec.p: No large, randomized trials have compared three or more tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) in a single chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) cohort. Most studies are two‐arm comparisons versus imatinib, or rely on indirect methods.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: A retrospective cohort study was conducted of 349 patients with chronic‐ and accelerated‐phase CML treated between 2007 and 2023 at Cleveland Clinic centers in Northeast Ohio. Overall survival (OS), event‐free survival (EFS), 12‐month therapeutic milestone achievement, and BCR‐ABL1 transcript decline velocity across first‐, second‐, and third‐line TKIs were compared. Baseline demographics, comorbidities, cytogenetics, and hematologic parameters were collected. Multivariable regression and time‐dependent Cox models were adjusted for confounders and varying therapy initiation times.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: First‐line TKIs included imatinib (53%), dasatinib (30%), nilotinib (15%), and bosutinib (2%). Median age ranged from 52 to 60 years, most patients were White, and high‐risk cytogenetics were rare. Five‐year OS ranged from 78% for dasatinib to 90% for nilotinib, with nilotinib associated with improved OS (hazard ratio [HR], 0.43) and EFS (HR, 0.48) and the fastest BCR‐ABL1 decline (β = −8.3%) versus imatinib. In second‐ (n = 181) and third‐line therapy (n = 91), no significant differences in outcomes were observed. Across all lines, time‐dependent modeling showed improved EFS only for nilotinib (HR, 0.61). Unadjusted OS was higher in patients starting treatment in 2007–2010 versus later periods but differences disappeared after adjustment.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Real‐world data indicate that imatinib achieves comparable response rates to newer TKIs, with durable survival. Nilotinib consistently shows faster BCR‐ABL1 decline and improved EFS overall, consistent with prior network meta‐analyses. Lack of improvement in OS over time suggests the need to investigate factors influencing long‐term outcomes in CML.

abstract.p: Among patients with chronic myeloid leukemia treated in routine clinical practice, imatinib achieved durable long‐term survival comparable to newer tyrosine kinase inhibitors. Nilotinib was associated with faster BCR‐ABL1 transcript decline and improved event‐free survival, which highlights potential differences in disease control despite similar overall outcomes.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: The management of chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) has evolved dramatically over the past several decades. In the early 1960s, it was managed symptomatically with cytoreductive therapies, followed by the use of interferon α and allogeneic stem cell transplantation in the 1980s and 1990s. 1 , 2 This approach persisted until 2001, when imatinib revolutionized the field and became widely regarded as the first small‐molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) in modern oncology. 3 Subsequently, several second‐ and third‐generation TKIs were developed and demonstrated efficacy in both first‐line and later line settings for the management of CML. 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 More recently, asciminib, an allosteric inhibitor of the BCR‐ABL1 fusion protein, was approved in the first‐line setting in 2024. 8 These major therapeutic advances have transformed CML from a uniformly fatal disease into a chronic condition associated with near‐normal life expectancy.

Despite the impressive response rates observed in clinical trials, real‐world management often differs. Response rates in routine clinical practice tend to be lower than those reported in controlled trial settings. 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 Therapy discontinuation is relatively common, and may occur for reasons other than treatment failure, including intolerance, comorbidities, and financial toxicity. 9 , 11 , 13 These factors frequently result in therapy switching. TKI cost represents a major financial burden to patients and can delay initiation and decrease adherence, which may affect survival and outcomes. 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 Hence, National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines (version 1.2026) recognized medication cost as independent of risk score, and noted that “the cost of generic TKIs can be substantially less than that of brand name TKIs” and that “the cost of treatment to both the patient and to society can be considered.”

A key challenge for hematologists is selecting the optimal TKI for newly diagnosed patients, particularly because most pivotal frontline trials have compared second‐ or third‐generation TKIs to imatinib, rather than conducting direct head‐to‐head comparisons among newer agents. To date, no large randomized trials have simultaneously compared three or more TKIs within the same cohort; available evidence is largely limited to indirect comparisons, such as network meta‐analyses. 19 , 20 This gap in evidence complicates treatment selection in routine clinical practice. To address this, we conducted a real‐world study evaluating the efficacy of TKIs and documenting rates of treatment discontinuation via a longitudinal design. Our study provides comparative data across all available TKIs within the same clinical setting. We also assessed TKI efficacy via velocity of BCR‐ABL1 transcript decline as a surrogate for response. Moreover, we compared survival between earlier and later therapeutic periods. This study examined imatinib efficacy by comparing outcomes from an era when it was the only available TKI to an era in which five different TKIs were in use, which allowed us to partially mitigate for confounding by indication. These findings may inform clinical decision‐making, particularly in resource‐limited settings or for patients facing financial constraints.

sec.title: Study design, setting, and participants
sec.p: We conducted a retrospective study to evaluate the efficacy of TKIs in chronic‐phase CML at Cleveland Clinic centers in Ohio, United States. The centers included the main referral hospital, regional hospitals, and satellite clinics encompassing Northeast Ohio. We included patients diagnosed with chronic‐ or accelerated‐phase CML between January 1, 2007, and January 1, 2023. Data were last updated in March 2025. We excluded patients who were in blast‐phase CML at the time of diagnosis. The study was reviewed and approved by the Cleveland Clinic Foundation (CCF) Institutional Review Board. Patient consent was waived by the CCF Institutional Review Board.

sec.title: Data source and measurements
sec.p: Patients were identified via the CCF cancer registry. Data were collected by physicians from electronic medical records and entered into a REDCap database. 21 Data quality was assessed via multiple methods, including built‐in REDCap validation checks, Excel‐based data verification, and biostatistical review. The data set underwent extensive quality review, and missing data were minimized via duplicate review.

Data were collected longitudinally from the time of CML diagnosis until the last follow‐up encounter. Variables collected included age; sex (self‐reported); race (self‐reported); comorbidities; smoking and alcohol use; CML phase; diagnosis date; complete blood count and differential at diagnosis and at response assessment; spleen size (when available); bone marrow biopsy results (when available); cytogenetic results; BCR‐ABL1 transcript measurements, including subtype (P190, P210, or P230); tyrosine kinase domain mutation analysis (when performed); next‐generation sequencing (when available); all treatment lines and corresponding responses; allogeneic transplantation (if done); and patient vital status.

Details regarding reasons for therapy discontinuation were also collected, including financial toxicity or intolerance, when reported. All approved TKIs were included in the analysis: imatinib, dasatinib, nilotinib, bosutinib, ponatinib, and asciminib.

CML phase (chronic, accelerated, or blast crisis) was defined according to the 2022 International Consensus Classification of Myeloid Neoplasms and Acute Leukemias. 22 High‐risk cytogenetics was defined as complex karyotype, +8, del(17) or abnormalities of 17p, +19, and inv(3)(q21.3q26.2) or t(3;3)(q21.3;q26.2). The full data repository is provided in Supplementary Material 2.

sec.title: CML response assessment
sec.p: Response to TKI therapy was determined via a milestone‐based approach modified from the 2024 NCCN milestone criteria (Figure 1). 23 Treatment response was assessed at the molecular level via the International Scale (IS), defined as the ratio of BCR‐ABL1 transcripts to ABL1 transcripts and expressed as a percentage on a logarithmic scale. 24 Major molecular response (MMR) (MR3) was defined as a BCR‐ABL1 transcript level of ≤0.1%, MR4 as ≤0.01%, and MR4.5 as ≤0.0032%.

caption.p: Response assessment of CML treated with tyrosine kinase inhibitors. CML indicates chronic myeloid leukemia; PCR, polymerase chain reaction.

sec.p: If a patient remained on the same TKI for less than 3 months, the response was considered nonevaluable. Molecular monitoring was performed at the discretion of the treating hematologist but was primarily conducted at 3, 6, and 12 months. 24 Treatment failure was defined as a BCR‐ABL1 transcript level of >10% at 3 months (which required confirmation within 1–3 months), >10% at 6 months, or >1% at 12 months. 24

Among patients who did not meet the criteria for treatment failure and who remained on therapy for approximately 1 year (window of 11–14 months) or longer, response assessment was based on the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) result closest to the 12‐month time point. For patients who remained on the same TKI for less than 11 months, response was determined via the last available PCR result before treatment discontinuation or switching.

For patients treated in earlier years of the cohort, response assessment was based on the criteria in use at that time. During these earlier years, normalized copy numbers were frequently used for response determination. Specifically, for the years preceding 2010, before widespread adoption of the IS, molecular response was categorized into three groups: complete molecular remission (undetectable BCR‐ABL1 transcripts), ≥3‐log reduction in BCR‐ABL1 transcripts, or <3‐log reduction. BCR‐ABL1 transcript measurements were obtained according to routine clinical practice, typically at 3‐month intervals.

sec.title: Outcomes and comparison groups
sec.p: We evaluated overall survival (OS), event‐free survival (EFS), 12‐month response rates, and BCR‐ABL1 transcript decline velocity among patients with CML treated with first‐line TKI therapy.

Because response assessment methodologies evolved over the study period, we harmonized response definitions into a unified binary framework to facilitate comparisons across treatment eras. This end point was termed 12‐month therapeutic milestone achievement (TMA). The response outcome was defined as achievement of a clinically meaningful molecular response at approximately 12 months (11‐ to 14‐month window), categorized as “milestone achieved” versus “milestone not achieved.” Patients who received less than 11 months of therapy were excluded from this analysis. For patients monitored via the IS, response achievement was defined as attainment of MMR (MR3; BCR‐ABL1, ≤0.1%). For patients treated before widespread adoption of the IS, response achievement was defined as either complete molecular remission (undetectable BCR‐ABL1 transcripts) or a ≥3‐log reduction in BCR‐ABL1 transcript levels, consistent with the contemporary standards at that time. In periods when cytogenetic assessment represented the primary response metric, complete cytogenetic response (CCyR) was considered equivalent to response achievement. Relapse in CML was defined by the loss of hematologic response, loss of CCyR or its molecular correlate (BCR‐ABL1, >1%), or a 1‐log increase in BCR‐ABL1 transcript levels with loss of MMR, as defined by 2024 NCCN guidelines. 23

These outcomes were also evaluated within the same cohort after second‐ and third‐line TKI therapy. To better isolate TKI efficacy in later line settings, patients who developed a BCR‐ABL1 tyrosine kinase domain resistance mutation were excluded to minimize confounding by indication. The choice of TKI and initial dosing was at the discretion of the treating hematologist, and generally aligned with Food and Drug Administration labeling, published hematology guidelines, and the potential side effect profile of each drug. No institutional protocol dictated TKI selection.
Last, we examined the survival of patients grouped into the following categories of year of diagnosis: 2007–2010, 2011–2014, 2015–2018, and 2019–2023.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Continuous variables were summarized as medians with interquartile ranges (IQRs), and categorical variables as counts with proportions. Time on first‐line therapy until treatment change was calculated in the subset of patients who were on a first‐line TKI and then went on to a second‐line TKI, from the start date of the first treatment line to the start date of the subsequent treatment line. Months of person‐time across the first three lines of therapy was determined by calculating the months on therapy in each line for each person and then summing across all lines within TKI type.

Time from the start of treatment line to evolution to accelerated or blast phase was estimated via the Kaplan–Meier method. Patients who experienced disease evolution were followed from the date of treatment line start to the date of disease evolution. Patients who had not yet evolved were censored at their date of last follow‐up. OS time was calculated from the date of treatment start to the date of death or last follow‐up, whichever came first. Stringent EFS was calculated from the date of treatment start to the first of death, treatment discontinuation for intolerance or financial toxicity (to the specific line), relapse (at any time), progression to accelerated or blast phase (at any time), or treatment failure (to the specific line). 8 Patients alive without event were censored at the last date of follow‐up. The Kaplan–Meier method estimated survival probabilities, and the log‐rank test was used to test for differences. Multivariable Cox regression adjusted for potential confounders was determined a priori and based on the number of events in each analysis. Further details on confounder selection are provided in Supplementary Material 2.

All BCR‐ABL1 transcript values measured during each line of treatment were plotted over time, from treatment start, and overlaid with a loess smooth for each treatment group to examine trends. Generalized linear mixed models with a random intercept to account for the correlation between multiple observations from the same patient over time were applied to see whether treatment was associated with change in BCR‐ABL1 level. A normal family with identity link was used. All statistical analyses were conducted with R, version 4.4.

sec.title: First‐line TKIs
sec.p: Of 371 patients, 349 were included in the initial cohort and analyzed. Figure S1 shows the flowchart for analyzed patients in the study. Table 1 summarizes the baseline characteristics of patients with CML treated with a first‐line TKI. Table S1 summarizes the frequency of use of each TKI in each line of therapy. Months of person‐time per TKI type were 10,450 for imatinib, 7648 for dasatinib, 6957 for nilotinib, 1471 for bosutinib, 876 for ponatinib, and 19 for asciminib. The prevalence of cardiovascular diseases was higher in patients treated with first‐line bosutinib compared to the other groups. The median time patients spent on a first‐line TKI before switching to a second‐line TKI was 15 months (IQR, 7–29 months) for imatinib, 12 months (IQR, 6–21 months) for dasatinib, 16 months (IQR, 10–33 months) for nilotinib, and 10 months (IQR, 3–28 months) for bosutinib (log‐rank p = .3). The time to evolution from chronic phase to accelerated or blast phase in each line is summarized in Table S2. The 12‐month TMA response rates were 27% (38 of 139 evaluable) for imatinib, 21% (16 of 75) for dasatinib, 30% (10 of 33) for nilotinib, and 40% (two of five) for bosutinib (p = .6). In the multivariable logistic regression model for 12‐month TMA response rates, there was no difference between TKIs (Table S3).

sec.p: The median follow‐up time among survivors, from first‐line treatment start, was 7.2 years (range, 0.5–16.9 years). During that time, 92 patients died from any cause, 43 from relapsed or progressive disease, 10 from transplantation, 37 from other causes, and two from unknown causes. The majority of patients who died from relapsed or progressive disease started first‐line therapy before 2015 (58%), and their median time from the start of first‐line therapy to death from disease was 3.8 years. Median, 2‐year, and 5‐year OS are summarized in Table 2. There was no difference in OS or EFS between different TKIs in the first‐line setting in the unadjusted analysis (Figure 2). In the multivariable regression model, only nilotinib was associated with improved OS compared to imatinib (hazard ratio [HR], 0.43; 95% CI, 0.21–0.88; overall p = .087; Table S4). Similarly, only nilotinib was associated with improved EFS compared to imatinib (HR, 0.48; 95% CI, 0.31–0.72; p = .002; Table S5). In the EFS multivariable regression model, increased monocytes and chronic heart failure were associated with worse outcomes. Throughout the cohort, a total of 34 patients received allogeneic transplantations at some point, with a median OS of 20 months (95% CI, 18–41 months).

sec.p: Regarding BCR‐ABL1 transcript kinetics, on average at any given point in time, nilotinib and dasatinib were associated with lower BCR‐ABL1 transcripts by the IS than imatinib (β = −8.3%; 95% CI, −15% to −2%; p = .01) (β = −5.6%; 95% CI, −11% to −0.46%; p = .03) (Tables S6 and S7; Figure S2).

sec.title: Second‐line TKIs
sec.p: In this analysis, 182 patients were studied. Table S8 summarizes baseline characteristics of the comparison groups. The 12‐month TMA response rates were 26% (six of 23 evaluable) for imatinib, 28% (12 of 43) for dasatinib, 30% (14 of 46) for nilotinib, 15% (two of 13) for bosutinib, 0% (zero of two) for ponatinib, and 0% (zero of one) for asciminib (p = 0.9). A multivariable logistic regression model for response rates was not done because of the low number of events.

The median follow‐up time among survivors, from second‐line treatment start, was 5.4 years (range, 0.3–15.3 years). During that time, 45 patients died from any cause, 23 from relapsed or progressive disease, eight from transplantation, 13 from other causes, and one from an unknown cause. OS and EFS estimates are summarized in Table 2. The 2‐year OS was numerically higher in nilotinib compared to dasatinib, imatinib, and bosutinib but the difference decreased at the 5‐year mark (Figure 3). The 2‐year EFS estimates were numerically higher in imatinib than dasatinib, nilotinib, or bosutinib (Figure 3). The multivariable regression model showed no difference in EFS hazard between comparison groups (Table S9). Higher basophils predicted worse EFS (p < .05). A multivariable Cox regression model for OS was not done because of the low number of events.

caption.p: Overall survival (A) and event‐free survival (B) of patients diagnosed with chronic‐ or accelerated‐phase chronic myeloid leukemia, stratified by the second‐line tyrosine kinase inhibitor used.

sec.p: Regarding BCR‐ABL1 transcript kinetics, on average at any given point in time, only bosutinib was associated with lower log10‐transformed BCR‐ABL1 transcripts by the IS than imatinib (β = 1.4%; 95% CI, 0.21–2.5; p = .02) (Table S10; Figure S3).

sec.title: Third‐line TKIs
sec.p: In this analysis, 91 patients were studied. Table S11 summarizes the baseline characteristics of the comparison groups. The 12‐month TMA response rates were 33% (four of 12 evaluable) for imatinib, 24% (four of 17) for dasatinib, 0% (zero of five) for nilotinib, 14% (one of seven) for bosutinib, 17% (one of six) for ponatinib, and not available for asciminib (p = .8). A multivariable logistic regression model was not done because of the low number of events.

The median follow‐up time among survivors, from third‐line treatment start, was 3.5 years (range, 0–12.6 years). During that time, 25 patients died from any cause, 13 from relapsed or progressive disease, five from transplantation, and seven from other causes. OS and EFS estimates are summarized in Table 2. The 2‐year OS was numerically lower in imatinib compared to other lines (Figure 4). The 2‐year EFS estimates were numerically higher in bosutinib and asciminib than in other TKIs (Figure 4). The multivariable regression model showed no difference in EFS hazard between comparison groups (Table S12), and could not be fit for OS because of low event numbers.

caption.p: Overall survival (A) and event‐free survival (B) of patients diagnosed with chronic‐ or accelerated‐phase chronic myeloid leukemia, stratified by the third‐line tyrosine kinase inhibitor used.

sec.p: Regarding BCR‐ABL1 transcript kinetics, there was no association between TKIs and BCR‐ABL1 transcripts by the IS (Table S13; Figure S4).

sec.title: Time‐dependent analysis of all TKIs
sec.p: In this analysis, we consider all lines of treatment with a time‐dependent covariate. Asciminib was excluded because of limited outcomes and follow‐up duration.

In this model, dasatinib and nilotinib were associated with numerically but not statistically improved OS compared with imatinib (Table S14). Nilotinib, compared to imatinib, was the only TKI associated with an improvement in EFS over time (time‐dependent HR, 0.61; 95% CI, 0.42–0.88; p = .008) (Table S15). Moreover, cumulative time on prior treatments is associated with significantly worse EFS.

sec.title: Survival of patients with CML grouped by year of diagnosis
sec.p: In the survival analyses of patients grouped into categories of year of treatment start, patients who started treatment in 2010 and before had improved OS but not EFS compared with patients who started treatment in 2011–2014, 2015–2018, and 2019 and later (log‐rank p = .01 and p = .08, respectively) (Figure 5). Tables S16 and S17 summarize unadjusted OS and EFS estimates. Tables S18 and S19 summarize adjusted regression models for OS and EFS estimates. Although OS and EFS hazards numerically increased for each additional year of increase in treatment start, these were not statistically significant.

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: In this study, our objective was to evaluate the real‐world effectiveness of TKI therapy in comparison to outcomes reported in clinical trials. We aimed to provide clinically relevant data to inform physicians practicing in resource‐limited settings, where treatment selection and monitoring strategies may differ from those in controlled trial environments. Additionally, we sought to examine the effectiveness of imatinib, the first approved TKI and the most widely accessible agent globally, given its continued use in many parts of the world.

The efficacy of second‐ and third‐generation TKIs, primarily demonstrated via comparisons with imatinib, has been established in randomized clinical trials. For example, the DASISION trial showed that dasatinib achieved higher rates of CCyR and MMR compared with imatinib, although OS (HR, 1.01; 95% CI, 0.6–1.7) and progression‐free survival (HR, 1.06; 95% CI, 0.7–1.7) were similar between treatment arms. 25 In contrast, our real‐world analysis did not identify significant differences in 12‐month TMA response rates and, in agreement with the DASISION study, observed no significant differences in OS or EFS. Several factors may explain these findings. First, outcomes in routine clinical practice often differ from those observed in clinical trials, where medication access is ensured, adherence is closely monitored, and enrolled patients typically have better performance status and fewer comorbidities. Second, although second‐generation TKIs may achieve faster or deeper molecular responses, potential differences in toxicity profiles and treatment‐related morbidity could attenuate long‐term survival advantages. Third, many of the pivotal frontline trials were open label, which may introduce performance or assessment bias. In the phase 3 ENESTnd trial, 846 patients with newly diagnosed chronic‐phase CML were randomized to receive nilotinib 300 mg twice daily (n = 282), nilotinib 400 mg twice daily (n = 281), or imatinib 400 mg once daily (n = 283). Nilotinib was associated with higher molecular remission rates and lower 24‐month CML‐related deaths but no significant differences in OS. 26 These results align with our results, where we found that first‐line nilotinib was associated with an improvement in EFS in adjusted analyses. We believe that this might be driven by improved leukemia control, as demonstrated by the faster decline in BCR‐ABL1 transcripts compared to imatinib. Our study found no differences between imatinib and bosutinib in OS, EFS, or BCR‐ABL1 decline velocity. The BFORE trial showed that MMR was higher in bosutinib but not EFS or OS. 27 The EPIC trial was a randomized, phase 3 trial designed to compare ponatinib 45 mg daily versus imatinib 400 mg daily in patients newly diagnosed with chronic‐phase CML. It found that MMR was higher in ponatinib numerically but not statistically; however, it was terminated early because of safety concerns. 28 Our study found that ponatinib was not superior to imatinib in survival outcomes in subsequent‐line settings nor time‐dependent analyses; however, these findings should be interpreted cautiously given the limited sample size. Both the PACE and OPTIC trials investigated the efficacy of ponatinib in the subsequent‐line setting via an uncontrolled design, and hence we cannot infer its efficacy compared to imatinib. 6 , 29 We had a limited number of patients treated with asciminib and only in the subsequent‐line setting, which is because asciminib was more recently approved and only approved for the first‐line setting in 2024. 8 In the phase 3 trial ASC4FIRST, asciminib was found to induce deeper responses than investigator‐selected TKIs but no differences were reported in OS or EFS.

There are no large, randomized trials directly comparing three or more TKIs simultaneously within the same cohort. All head‐to‐head comparisons have been conducted as two‐arm trials against imatinib, whereas comparisons among newer agents rely on indirect methods, such as network meta‐analyses or few observational data. Hence, our study contributes to addressing a critical gap in the literature. In a network meta‐analysis of 13 randomized trials (n = 5079 patients) evaluating imatinib, nilotinib, dasatinib, bosutinib, radotinib, and ponatinib, investigators reported that nilotinib was superior to other TKIs. 20 In another network meta‐analysis of 21 randomized controlled trials (n = 10,187 patients), nilotinib (300 or 400 mg twice daily), dasatinib (100 mg every day), and radotinib (300 mg twice daily) were identified as the most efficacious TKIs. 19 Additionally, in a multicenter Italian Network/CML Campus prospective cohort study of consecutive patients with newly diagnosed chronic‐phase CML, 702 patients received frontline imatinib and 731 received second‐generation TKIs (nilotinib, 414; dasatinib, 312; bosutinib, 5). 12 Although faster responses were observed with the second‐generation TKIs compared with imatinib, long‐term clinical outcomes were similar. However, the results were not stratified according to the specific TKI administered, which limits direct comparison with our findings. Definitive determination of whether nilotinib is superior to other TKIs would require a pragmatic, multiarm study with extended follow‐up, which ideally would approach at least 5 years. It is important to note that the above network meta‐analysis found that nilotinib was associated with higher response rates and improved efficacy end points 19 , 20 ; however, OS was not specifically evaluated. These higher response rates are consistent with the improved EFS observed in our study and in the ENESTnd trial. 26 In contrast, the OS benefit observed in our study was less pronounced than the EFS benefit, and was not replicated in the ENESTnd trial. Several factors may explain this discrepancy, including the increased risk of cardiovascular adverse events associated with nilotinib, the impact of effective salvage therapies after imatinib failure, and the high treatment discontinuation rates observed in both groups (approximately 25% in both groups at the 2‐year mark). Because of this, the OS benefit with nilotinib seen in our study should be interpreted cautiously. Although MMR was used as a surrogate end point in registrational trials, long‐term follow‐up across randomized studies has consistently demonstrated no significant difference in OS among TKIs. One possible explanation is that the incremental improvements in leukemia control achieved with second‐ and third‐generation TKIs may be offset by differences in non–leukemia‐related mortality, which thereby attenuated survival differences over time. Additionally, we found that 12‐month TMA response rates and stringent EFS estimates in TKIs were low, and did not parallel OS outcomes. This discrepancy may reflect the imperfect correlation between surrogate end points and long‐term survival, particularly given that TKIs remain highly effective even when predefined molecular milestones are not achieved. Furthermore, in real‐world practice, patients with suboptimal responses are not always switched immediately to an alternative TKI, which may further weaken the association between early response metrics and OS. Our EFS estimates were lower than those reported in clinical trials and closer to observational cohorts. This discrepancy likely reflects the realities of routine clinical practice, including greater heterogeneity in patient characteristics and management patterns. Furthermore, we applied stringent event definitions. The definition of EFS in CML has evolved toward more rigorous criteria over time, 30 which results in increased event capture and consequently lower EFS estimates in newer studies. For example, in the IRIS study, EFS was defined from the time of treatment initiation to any of the following: loss of complete hematologic response, loss of major cytogenetic response, progression to accelerated or blast phase, or death from any cause at any time while in the study. 31 On the other hand, in ENESTnd, the end points of EFS were loss of response (complete hematologic, partial cytogenetic, or CCyR), progression to accelerated or blast phase, or death from any cause while on treatment. More recently, in the ASC4FIRST trial, a definition of EFS was used similar to our study. 8

Our study found that OS was very high for patients diagnosed with CML before 2010, by reaching 85% at the 9‐year mark, and did not improve in more recent years compared with those diagnosed in earlier years. This could be related to several hypotheses: (1) life expectancy in the United States has declined in the last several years, influenced by multiple factors 32 , 33 , 34 ; (2) possible higher toxicity‐related mortality from second‐ and third‐generation TKIs compared with imatinib; (3) the use of strict milestones for response assessment with TKIs, which leads to early switching and potential therapy interruptions, which may worsen long‐term outcomes 35 , 36 ; and (4) second‐ and third‐generation TKIs are more expensive, which can result in financial toxicity for patients. Our study was not designed to determine the underlying cause of these observations, and other explanations remain possible. In a Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) analysis done in 2023, the 5‐year OS was 82% in 2005–2009 and 78% in 2010–2014 but not reported in 2015–2019. 37 Data obtained from the SEER database estimated a 5‐year relative survival of 63.1% for the period 2005–2008, 69.7% for 2009–2015, and 71.1% for 2016–2022, 38 , 39 which indicates that the gain in survival has largely plateaued in recent years, consistent with our findings. We found that imatinib was associated with excellent long‐term outcomes when used in the first‐, second‐, or third‐line setting among patients with CML without resistance mutations. These findings are particularly relevant in an era of rising medication costs and increasing insurance‐related barriers to access. Our results show that imatinib remains a highly effective option in appropriate patients, and provide reassurance to clinicians when access to newer, more expensive agents is limited.

Our study has several limitations. As an observational analysis, it is inherently subject to residual confounding. Spleen size was not included in the multivariable models because it was not consistently documented for all patients. Baseline cytogenetic risk was also excluded from the regression analyses because of small subgroup sizes. Although our cohort reflects real‐world practice across multiple hospitals and clinics in Northeast Ohio, this remains a single‐institution experience and therefore has limited external validity. Additionally, certain subgroups, particularly first‐line bosutinib and subsequent‐line asciminib and ponatinib, were small, which reflects real‐world prescribing patterns in which clinicians may preferentially continue therapies with which they are most familiar. We used a time‐dependent Cox model to address this issue, which confirmed our findings in the first‐, second‐, and third‐line comparisons. Despite the collection of extensive baseline and longitudinal data, the number of covariates included in the multivariable models was restricted by statistical considerations and sample size constraints. Although it would be of interest to apply propensity score weighting or marginal structural Cox regression models in a retrospective treatment comparison of this type, the small number of patients in some of the treatment groups precludes fitting the models to estimate propensity scores. Another limitation is that we did not include the dose of TKIs in the analysis, given the complexity of such a design. Because response criteria have changed over time, we used modified criteria to account for these changes, which reflected best practices at the time of therapy administration.

Our study also has several important strengths. To our knowledge, this is the first longitudinal analysis comparing TKI prescribing patterns and outcomes across first‐, second‐, and third‐line settings within a single cohort. The longitudinal design minimizes selection bias and enhances comparability by applying a uniform data collection framework and consistent analytic approach across treatment lines. Additionally, this is, to our knowledge, the first study to evaluate all available TKIs, head to head, within a single analytic model, rather than relying on indirect comparisons. We incorporated BCR‐ABL1 kinetics evaluation and time‐dependent modeling to further strengthen our conclusions. The 16‐year study period spans the evolution of the TKI era, from the imatinib‐only period to the introduction of multiple next‐generation agents, which enables assessment across distinct therapeutic eras. Finally, the cohort features one of the longest median follow‐up durations reported in the literature, and rigorous data quality procedures were implemented to ensure analytic validity.

In conclusion, our study demonstrates that imatinib provides response rates comparable to newer TKIs and is associated with prolonged survival in patients with CML, whether used as first‐ or subsequent‐line therapy across different therapeutic eras. First‐line nilotinib was the only TKI associated with improved OS and EFS compared with imatinib. Although 12‐month TMA response rates and EFS appeared relatively low, OS among TKI‐treated patients remained high, which suggests that these surrogate outcomes may not fully capture the underlying disease biology or long‐term clinical benefit. Notably, OS for patients diagnosed with CML between 2007 and 2011 was high and did not improve over the course of our study period, which highlights the need to verify this finding and investigate its underlying causes. Future studies should prioritize well‐powered, multiarm pragmatic trial designs with OS as the primary end point to definitively assess comparative effectiveness and identify the least toxic TKIs.
